nameStory: This St. John's wort gets its name from the 'majus' part of its scientific name, which means 'larger' in Latin - it's one of the bigger members of the Canadian St. John's wort group. The St. John's wort family name comes from the tradition of gathering these yellow-flowered plants around St. John's Day (June 24th), when many species are in peak bloom.
description: Large Canadian St. John's wort is a perennial wildflower that stands out among its smaller cousins with its relatively robust size. Like other St. John's worts, it produces cheerful yellow flowers with five petals and numerous thread-like stamens that give the blooms a fuzzy, sunburst appearance. This native North American plant grows in an upright habit, branching from the base, and can be found scattered across New England's wetlands and moist areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with 5 petals and a burst of yellow stamens in the center, creating a star-like appearance. The flowers feel delicate and papery when touched, and bloom in small clusters at the stem tips.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. Hold a leaf up to the light and you may see tiny translucent dots scattered throughout - these oil glands are a St. John's wort trademark.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows larger and more robust than many other native St. John's worts, with multiple branching stems forming a somewhat bushy appearance. The stems feel smooth and slightly ridged to the touch.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: After flowering, develops small, egg-shaped seed capsules that split into three parts when ripe. The capsules start green and turn brown, making a soft rattling sound when dry and shaken.

habitat: Large Canadian St. John's wort prefers moist to wet soils in marshes, swamp edges, wet meadows, and along stream banks throughout New England. You'll often find it growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other moisture-loving plants in areas that stay damp through most of the growing season. It thrives in both sunny and partially shaded wetland environments.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small, opposite leaves on reddish stems. The plant begins to establish its branching structure but won't yet show flower buds.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers opening in sunny weather. Fresh flowers appear continuously through much of the summer, attracting small bees and flies.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature, turning from green to brown. The foliage may take on reddish or bronze tints before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground as a perennial herb. Only dried seed capsules on dead stems may remain visible above the snow.

funFact: St. John's worts have been used medicinally for over 2,000 years, and scientists have discovered that those tiny translucent dots you can see in the leaves contain concentrated oils that glow red when crushed - earning some species the nickname 'blood herb' in medieval times.
confusionNotes: With 16 different St. John's wort species in New England, telling them apart can be tricky! Focus on size (this one is larger than most natives), habitat (it loves wet feet while Common St. John's wort prefers dry areas), and leaf shape. Remember: wet habitat usually means native species, dry roadsides usually mean the weedy European Common St. John's wort.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Canadian' St. John's wort, this plant is native throughout much of North America, not just Canada. The name reflects early botanical naming conventions rather than its actual geographic range, which extends well into the United States including all of New England.
compareHints: Large Canadian St. John's wort lives up to its name by being more robust than its close relative Canada St. John's wort (Hypericum canadense), which is much smaller and more delicate. Unlike the weedy Common St. John's wort that dominates roadsides, this native species sticks to wetlands and has a less aggressive spreading habit. The wet habitat preference is the easiest way to distinguish it from most of its relatives.
